What Makes an Efficient VLA? Navigating Action-Head Design, Scaling, and Latency

Luoyang Sun ††thanks: Equal contribution. Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications    Fengfa Li Affiliation: Li Auto Inc.    Lei Ren ††thanks: Project Leader.††thanks: Corresponding author Affiliation: Li Auto Inc.    Xinyu Cui Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences Affiliation: University of Chinese Academy of Sciences    Haifeng Zhang 33footnotemark: 3 Affiliation: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences    Fangxiang Feng Affiliation: School of Artificial Intelligence, Beijing University of Posts and Telecommunications    Kaike Zhang Affiliation: Li Auto Inc.    Kun Zhan Affiliation: Li Auto Inc.    Yan Xie Affiliation: Li Auto Inc.    Jun Wang Affiliation: University College London    Cheng Deng 33footnotemark: 3 Affiliation: University of Edinburgh
Abstract

Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models combine a pretrained vision encoder, a language backbone, and an action head, but the relative contribution of these design choices has not been established under controlled, latency-paired conditions. We fix the backbone families (SigLIP2 and Qwen2.5) and the training pipeline, while sweeping action-head design and module scale, pairing every configuration with measured on-device latency. The study yields three findings. First, action-head performance is governed primarily by initialization rather than decoder architecture, loss, or inference budget: copying the last transformer layers of the language backbone into the head is the single largest lever we measure, at no latency cost, and the only axis that consistently improves performance across all module scales tested within the L1 family. Alignment also accounts for the other axes: flow matching and a heavier decoder pay off only while the head is misaligned and reverse once it is aligned, and additional inference passes provide no measurable benefit, suggesting that the additional expressiveness compensates for the alignment the head lacks. We read the mechanism as representation transfer. The aligned head keeps reading the instruction the way the backbone does, attending to the object nouns that name the task and staying aligned with the backbone in weight space, so it preserves instruction-grounding behavior associated with the backbone instead of relearning to act from scratch. Because we reach alignment only through initialization, we offer this as the account that best organizes the measurements rather than as a demonstrated cause, and we name the control that would settle it. Second, capacity only pays after alignment: the action head is the highest-return module to scale, but only once it is aligned. Third, those returns diminish sharply at a model size close to the one today’s π\pi-series VLAs already use, so further growth buys little in-domain accuracy for its added latency. The three together specify EffVLA, a compact model that matches the strongest open-source VLAs on standard LIBERO, leads on most LIBERO-Plus perturbation axes at lower latency, and transfers to a real SO-ARM101 arm with the recipe unchanged (only the training data is swapped).

Keywords: Vision-Language-Action model, Robot, Efficient inference

Code: https://github.com/MindVLA-Team/EFFVLA

Project Page: https://mindvla-team.github.io/EFFVLA

1 Introduction

A Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model is assembled from three components: a pretrained vision encoder, a pretrained language backbone, and an action head that turns their representations into motor commands. How to assemble them is largely decided by trial and error. π0\pi_{0} [2] builds a flow-matching action expert that runs several denoising steps; OpenVLA-OFT [11] replaces it with an MLP regression head reading VLM hidden states; OpenVLA [12] decodes action tokens autoregressively through the language backbone; FAST [26] puts a frequency-domain tokenizer in front of the same idea. Each system fixes a different combination of choices, trains on different data, and reports gains on a different benchmark. The field has accumulated improvements without controlled isolation of the contribution of each design choice. And because a VLA must act in real time, with only tens of milliseconds per action chunk, the latency cost of each choice matters as much as its accuracy, yet it is almost never reported.

This paper provides that measurement. We hold the backbone fixed (Qwen2.5-3B [33] with SigLIP2-So400m [34]), the pipeline fixed (DROID [10] pretraining, then LIBERO [20] fine-tuning), and the protocol fixed (LIBERO-Plus [6]), and we train 6363 cells that vary only the design under study. The study differs from prior design-space sweeps [16, 11] in two ways. First, every cell is paired with wall-clock latency on the same hardware (NVIDIA RTX 5090, bf16, action chunk size 8). Second, the four action-head axes that prior work varies jointly, decoder architecture, training loss, weight initialization, and number of inference passes, are isolated one at a time, so each contribution can be read without confounds. We analyze the action head first, then fix its best form and scale the three modules independently.

We call a fixed choice of the four action-head axes, independent of module size, a substrate. The analysis yields three design rules that compose directly into a recipe, answering in turn what to build, where to scale, and how big to make the model.

What to build. One axis dominates the rest, and it is not an architectural one: how the action head is initialized. Copying the last few transformer layers of the language backbone into the head, rather than training it from scratch, adds 7.17.1 points on LIBERO-Plus at no measurable latency cost (more than three times what scaling the language backbone across our full sweep buys), and it pays at every module scale we test within the L1 family. Once the head is aligned, the additional modeling complexity provides no further measurable gain: flow matching loses 4.44.4 points to plain L1, an elaborate decoder is no better than a single transformer block, and extra inference passes add nothing. Equivalently, the decoder and loss help only while the head is misaligned, where they partially compensate for the absence of VLM initialization, and the extra passes never help at all. Rule 1: align the head with the backbone by initializing it from the backbone’s last layers, and keep the rest simple, single-pass L1 regression.

Where to scale. Capacity only pays once the head is aligned, and that decides where added compute is worth spending. Under the aligned head, scaling the action head returns about four success-rate points per millisecond of added latency, against roughly 11 for the vision encoder and 0.150.15 for the language backbone; remove the initialization and the same head-scaling yields about a third as much (+3.1+3.1 points from ss to ll under random init versus +9.4+9.4 under VLM-init). the action head therefore offers the highest return on additional capacity, but only because, being aligned, it extends the language backbone’s computation rather than having to relearn it. Rule 2: align first, then spend the scaling budget on the action head.

How big. Further scaling provides no measurable benefit beyond a modest size. Scaling any of the three modules past our largest configuration leaves accuracy flat while latency keeps rising: the returns the first two rules identify are already captured at about 3.753.75B parameters, close to the budget the π\pi-series of VLAs [2] consistently adopts. Rule 3: stop there; within our tested regime, further scaling buys little in-domain accuracy for its added latency.

What this paper contributes is not a new architecture but a controlled account of what governs a modular VLA. Its centerpiece is that the dominant axis is how the action head is initialized, not the decoder, loss, or inference budget the literature has focused on. We read that effect at the representation level: attention and weight-space (CKA) analyses show that the initialized head keeps reading the instruction the way the backbone does, inheriting the VLM’s grounding instead of relearning to act from scratch, and the axes the literature tunes pay only while that inheritance is missing. Representation alignment is the account we offer for why initialization behaves this way. Because we can manipulate it only through initialization, we present it as the reading that best organizes the measurements rather than as an established cause, and we name the control that would test it (Section 8). The two scaling rules and the EffVLA recipe follow from the measurements and are consistent with that account. In summary, this paper makes the following contributions:

  • •

    We conduct a controlled, latency-paired study that isolates the four action-head axes and three module-scale axes one at a time, so that each measured gain is attributable to the design choice that changed rather than to a stronger backbone, more data, or a different benchmark.

  • •

    We identify the action head’s weight initialization, copying the backbone’s last transformer layers into the head, as the most influential axis in our controlled comparisons: it is positive in every matched L1 configuration we test and reorders the other axes, since the decoder and loss axes reverse sign between the initialized and the randomly initialized head while the inference-budget axis stops paying altogether. We read the effect at the representation level (attention and weight-space CKA analysis): the initialized head keeps reading the instruction the way the backbone does and stays close to it in weight space, where a random head does neither. Because we reach that state only through initialization, we offer representation alignment as the account that best organizes the measurements rather than as a demonstrated cause, and we name the control that would settle it.

  • •

    We show that capacity pays only after alignment: the action head is then the highest-return module to scale, buying more accuracy per unit of latency than the vision encoder or language backbone, while the same scaling on a misaligned head buys about a third as much.

  • •

    We show that these returns saturate at a modest, π\pi-series-sized budget, and distil the three findings into EffVLA, which matches the strongest open-source VLAs on standard LIBERO, leads on most LIBERO-Plus perturbation axes at lower latency, and transfers unchanged to a real SO-ARM101 arm.

2 Related Work

Vision-Language-Action models.

VLAs produce actions in three ways: decoding them as language tokens through the backbone (RT-1/RT-2 [4, 3], OpenVLA [12], FAST [26]); generating them with diffusion or flow matching, trading inference passes for expressiveness (Diffusion Policy [5], Octo [32], π0\pi_{0} [2], CogACT [15], GR00T N1 [1], Gemini Robotics [31]); or regressing them with a lightweight head, either directly from visual features (ACT [39]) or from VLM hidden states (OpenVLA-OFT [11]). Each arrived on its own backbone, data, and benchmark, so the three families have never been compared like-for-like, which Sections 3–6 do.

VLA design studies.

Closest to us, RoboVLMs [16] compares backbones and policy-head structures, OpenVLA-OFT [11] ablates loss and decoding on throughput grounds, and TinyVLA [35] targets the small-parameter regime. Concurrent design-space studies VLANeXt [36] and StarVLA-α\alpha [38] likewise revisit VLA design choices on LIBERO/LIBERO-Plus under unified protocols, the former distilling a recipe from a broad set of findings and the latter stripping complexity to isolate a few axes. Our study is distinguished by doing two things at once that, to our knowledge, no prior or concurrent VLA design study does together: it isolates action-head weight initialization as its own axis, the choice we find shapes the rest of the design (Section 3), and it pairs every design choice with measured wall-clock latency on a common deployment target. VLANeXt and StarVLA-α\alpha vary many choices jointly and on accuracy alone; our contribution is the controlled, latency-paired isolation rather than a new head.

Representation alignment and cross-module transfer.

That a module works best when it stays aligned with the pretrained representation it extends is a known lever: Kumar et al. [13] show naive fine-tuning can distort pretrained features when the objective competes with them, which is the regime a randomly initialized action head starts in, learning to read the backbone and to act at the same time. Lee et al. [14] show that fine-tuning a few layers can beat the full network. Copying the language backbone’s last layers into the action head initializes the head from the backbone’s representation space; it is the highest-return choice in the L1 family, while under flow matching it mildly hurts (−2.2-2.2 points).

Latency-aware design and scaling.

Hardware-aware architecture design has long optimized models against measured deployment cost rather than FLOPs alone (EfficientNet [29], MobileNet [8], MnasNet [28]). Representative systems efforts further demonstrate that substantial efficiency gains can come from hardware-conscious execution, including precision-aware acceleration in SPARK [22] and adaptive Transformer inference in ASTER [21], and roofline-based hardware co-design scaling for on-device LLMs [27]. Scaling laws further characterize parameter–data trade-offs in monolithic backbones [9, 7] and across robot embodiments and data volumes [24, 18]. We bring this measurement-driven Pareto framing to modular VLA design (Section 5), reporting per-module returns against measured on-device latency as descriptive slopes within our tested range rather than power-law fits.

3 The Four Action-Head Axes

The action head is where modular VLAs differ most, and where the literature offers the least controlled guidance. This section isolates the choices that define it. We describe the design space and protocol, then read off the axis that dominates the rest, the action head’s weight initialization, and show that it reorders the preferred value of every other axis.

Design space.

A modular VLA pairs a pretrained vision encoder (VV) and language backbone (LL) with an action head (AA). We fix the pair to SigLIP2 [34] and Qwen2.5 [33] and vary the action head along four independent axes:

  • •

    decoder: an MLP regression head on VLM hidden states, a stack of transformer blocks reading the backbone through a KV-share interface, or an autoregressive trunk that decodes action tokens through the language backbone itself;

  • •

    loss: L1 regression, flow matching [19, 23], or next-token prediction for the AR trunk;

  • •

    initialization (transformer-block heads only): random, or copied from the last transformer layers of the language backbone (VLM-init);

  • •

    inference passes: one forward pass per chunk, or four (denoising steps for flow matching; the same block re-run four times for L1).

In the L1L_{1} substrates the transformer block is the standard attention-plus-MLP block, so the random and VLM-init conditions share an identical architecture and the initialization contrast varies weights alone. Table 1 names the eight substrates (fixed choices of the four axes) we use as shorthand throughout.

Protocol and conventions.

Every cell follows the same two-stage pipeline: action-head pretraining on DROID [10] with public SigLIP2 and Qwen2.5 checkpoints, then full-VLA fine-tuning on LIBERO [20] with all backbones unfrozen. Evaluation is on LIBERO-Plus [6] (four task suites ×\times seven zero-shot perturbation axes, ∼1000{\sim}1000 rollouts per cell); the metric is success rate. Latency is end-to-end on an NVIDIA RTX 5090 (bf16, batch 11, action chunk size 88, torch.compile, mean of 100100 runs), the target recent VLA work reports against [12, 2, 11]. Three conventions hold everywhere and we state them once. First, each per-cell success rate averages ∼1000{\sim}1000 LIBERO-Plus rollouts, so its binomial standard error is ≈1.4{\approx}1.4 points; we treat success-rate differences below ∼1{\sim}1 point (and latency differences below 11 ms) as within measurement noise, and read gaps of only a few points as suggestive rather than decisive. This bounds evaluation variance; the per-axis and per-suite breakdowns (Tables 3, 6) use a fraction of these rollouts, so their standard error is correspondingly larger (a few points) and single-axis leads should be read with that in mind. Second, we sweep VV, LL, and AA over three sizes s<m<ls\!<\!m\!<\!l (with ll the anchor), plus a larger probe gg used only to test saturation (Section 5): Vs,m,l,g=86/307/400M/∼1BV_{s,m,l,g}=86/307/400\text{M}/{\sim}1\text{B} and Ls,m,l,g=0.5/1.5/3/7L_{s,m,l,g}=0.5/1.5/3/7B, while the transformer action head grows from {1,3,4}\{1,3,4\} blocks (∼0.35{\sim}0.35B at ll) to ∼0.65{\sim}0.65B at gg; the MLP head is the sole exception, scaling over 10/30/8010/30/80M (s/m/ls/m/l) with no gg. We trained 6363 cells (the design space is not a flat product across substrates because the action-head sizes differ per substrate, so we report the actual cell count rather than a full-grid fraction), prioritizing the largest-scale anchor for every substrate and the per-module sweeps used in Sections 3 and 5; protocol and grid details are in Appendix A through C.

Among the factors we isolate, initialization produces the largest and most consistent difference. Three rows of Table 1 make the point. Autoregressive action decoding incurs substantial latency relative to its measured accuracy: the autoregressive trunk (Fast) trails every parallel-decoding head by at least 1515 points and runs nearly 5×5\times slower. A plain MLP head (OFT) already lands within 11 point of the best cell (it reads VLM hidden states rather than the backbone’s KV cache, so this MLP-vs-transformer contrast also spans the read interface, which we hold fixed only across the four transformer-block substrates; Appendix N). And stacking transformer blocks helps only when they are initialized from the language backbone: random initialization costs 6.36.3 points, VLM-init recovers all of it. Flow matching, despite running four inference passes through the head, does not reach the best L1 score at this scale. But these contrasts are entangled: once the AR trunk is set aside, the sign of every remaining axis depends on which others are held fixed, so we disentangle them next.

To disentangle them, Table 2 reorganizes the pairwise contrasts of Table 1 by the axis each isolates, and the asymmetry is stark, though its two sides are not equally well resolved, so we read each against the ≈1.4{\approx}1.4-point evaluation error. What is unambiguous is the aligned column: once the head is initialized from the backbone, no axis buys anything. A transformer decoder over an MLP is worth +0.8+0.8 (0.60.6 error units, i.e. nothing), a fourth pass −0.2-0.2 (nothing), and flow matching reduces success rate by 4.44.4 points relative to four-pass L1 (3.13.1 evaluation-error units).

The misaligned column is where the additional complexity provides measurable gains: dropping the transformer decoder there costs 6.36.3 points (4.54.5 units), and flow matching and a fourth pass return +2.6+2.6 and +2.1+2.1, gains we read as real in direction but modest in size, at 1.91.9 and 1.51.5 error units. So the loss axis reverses sign outright, the decoder axis goes from a large penalty to nothing, and the compute axis simply stops paying; what they share is that all of them matter only while the head is misaligned. Within the L1 family, initialization is the exception in the opposite direction: it is positive in every matched comparison, worth +4.8+4.8 to +7.1+7.1 points at the anchor-scale substrates, and is the single largest and best-resolved effect in the table. Under flow matching, however, the same initialization reduces performance by 2.22.2 points, so we scope the initialization rule accordingly.

One explanation covers this pattern. Every axis that reverses adds expressive capacity to the head: a generative loss, a second pass through the same blocks, more decoder machinery. Each pays only while the head is initialized at random, and once the head is VLM-initialized, these additional mechanisms provide no further measurable gain and it becomes pure latency. These results suggest that the dominant limitation is compatibility with the backbone representation rather than insufficient expressiveness. A random head must discover how to read the backbone while it also learns to act, and the expressive machinery partially compensates for that.

The same explanation covers the apparent exception in Table 1, where a head with far less capacity than any transformer stack lands within a point of the best cell at the same latency. The MLP is the one substrate that never has to learn how to read the backbone: it consumes the VLM’s hidden states directly instead of attending to its KV cache, so no initialization-sensitive attention interface exists and there is no attention pattern to inherit. This direct readout is also why VLM-init does not apply to it. Its price appears in Section 5: with no depth to grow, it is the one substrate that cannot turn added capacity into accuracy. Section 4 makes the account measurable.

This reading is operational: three of the four axes have no best value in the abstract, since their preferred setting is induced once initialization is chosen, whereas initialization is decided on its own merits and is the largest lever we measure. Section 6 therefore adopts its best L1 setting, VLM-init.

No substrate wins on every axis, and the perturbation axes are where the heads diverge. Table 3 breaks the rollouts down two ways: on the four standard task suites the substrates are close, but on the seven perturbation axes the pure MLP head (OFT) is the most robust to sensor noise and lighting, while OFT-TF-vlminit leads on exactly the spatial–language axes a language-initialized head should help (camera viewpoint, language instructions, object layout). The autoregressive trunk (Fast) collapses specifically on the spatially demanding axes (initial state, camera, noise), where decoding actions token-by-token loses the spatial information the parallel heads retain.

4 The Alignment Mechanism

VLM initialization preserves substantially greater similarity to the language backbone than random initialization. Measuring the linear CKA between the action head and the corresponding backbone layers on the V=L=A=lV\!=\!L\!=\!A\!=\!l cells, the language-initialized head holds a CKA of 0.760.76 with the backbone throughout fine-tuning while a randomly initialized head never rises above 0.240.24 (Figure 2a), and the same separation holds at every layer of the head, where the aligned head sits near 0.760.76 from the backbone-facing layer to the action output while a random head stays near 0.240.24 throughout (Figure 2b). This representation similarity coincides with a consistent success-rate advantage: the success-rate advantage over random initialization holds across all six vision- and language-backbone sizes (Figure 2c). The inherited alignment also shows up in behaviour, as language grounding: told to “put the black bowl in the bottom drawer of the cabinet,” the aligned head concentrates on the instruction and on the bowl it names, while a random head is diffuse and leaves the instruction almost unattended (Figure 3, text mass 0.2230.223 vs. 0.0300.030; across 128128 rollouts the aligned head places about four times as much attention on the instruction text). The account matches the cross-module transfer of Section 2 and explains why the gains concentrate on the spatial and language perturbation axes (Table 3).

Both readings hold in aggregate, not just on the rollout of Figure 3. Over all 128128 rollouts (6464 per condition, spanning the four task suites) the VLM-init head places roughly four times as much attention mass on the instruction as the random head (per-rollout mean 0.2330.233 vs. 0.0550.055), and the two distributions do not overlap on a single rollout (Figure 4a). Ranking instruction words by the attention the aligned head gives them, the top of the list is the object and location nouns that name the task (stove, rack, cookie, alphabet, juice), each receiving several times the mass the random head assigns it (Figure 4b). The aligned head does not merely look at the instruction more; it looks at the part of the instruction that specifies the goal. Appendix L reports further rollouts and the token-level detail.

5 Module Scaling and Saturation

With the substrate fixed, where should extra compute go? We ask which module’s capacity improves accuracy (Figure 5) and where a unit of latency is best spent (Figure 6), sweeping VV, LL, AA at {s,m,l}\{s,m,l\} for the three deployment-relevant substrates (OFT, OFT-TF-vlminit, π0\pi_{0}; the Pareto-dominated random-init control is omitted). Both answers depend on the substrate and point to the same operating size; Appendix D gives the endpoint deltas and their ratio ρ\rho (success points per ms).

Consider capacity first. Extra action-head parameters raise accuracy only under VLM-init: the vision encoder and language backbone trace the same saturating curve under every substrate, and the substrates separate only on the action head (Figure 5, right), where scaling AA from ss to ll adds 9.49.4 points under OFT-TF-vlminit, essentially nothing under OFT (an MLP with no depth to grow), and 4.74.7 under π0\pi_{0}. This is the scaling-time counterpart of Finding 1: a head aligned with the language backbone turns capacity into accuracy, because the parameters extend a computation it already shares; under random initialization, the same capacity yields substantially smaller accuracy gains, because it must spend that capacity relearning the interface first.

Capacity is not the same as cost, so we turn to latency. On the accuracy–latency plane (Figure 6) the action head has the steepest trade-off under our recipe, 2.42.4 ms for 9.49.4 points, against 3.43.4 for the vision encoder and under 22 for the language backbone; the ordering A>V>LA\!>\!V\!>\!L holds across the shared latency span without extrapolating a rate. Because the substrate runs a single forward pass, latency rises monotonically with scale, free of the π0\pi_{0} depth–width inversion (Appendix D).

These sweeps deliberately stop at ll, because pushing past it adds nothing. Under OFT-TF-vlminit, enlarging the action head from ll (350350M) to gg (650650M) moves LIBERO-Plus success rate from 79.8%79.8\% to 78.3%78.3\%; a 11B vision encoder scores 78.9%78.9\% and a 77B language backbone 77.8%77.8\%, all within noise of or below ll (Figure 5, rightmost; Appendix D). Accuracy has saturated while latency would only keep climbing, so ll sits at the efficiency–accuracy knee, close to the budget the π\pi-series of VLAs [2] consistently adopts. In this model family and benchmark, our measurements place the saturation point at roughly the same scale. EffVLA (Section 6) is fixed at this scale.

One ordering follows from all of this: the substrate must be chosen before module sizes, since it decides whether action-head capacity is worth buying at all. For the VLM-init substrate, the action head provides the steepest measured accuracy–latency trade-off, under any other it shifts to vision then language, and beyond ll none of them buys much. The per-axis breakdown of which perturbations each module helps is in Appendix C (Table 6).

6 EffVLA: The Recipe the Rules Select

The recipe.

The analysis specifies one model. EffVLA is a 44-layer transformer-block action head copied from the last 44 transformer layers of Qwen2.5-3B and trained with single-pass L1 regression (Finding 1), reading the backbone through a KV-share interface on a SigLIP2-So400m vision encoder at 256256-pixel input. The action head contributes ∼0.35{\sim}0.35B of the model’s ∼3.75{\sim}3.75B parameters, reflecting the allocation favored by the module-scaling study (Findings 2 and 3). End-to-end latency is 39.239.2 ms per action chunk on an RTX 5090, and nothing in the architecture is tuned beyond what the three rules select. Training follows the two-stage pipeline of Section 3; full hyperparameters are in Appendix A.

Open-source baselines on LIBERO and LIBERO-Plus.

On the saturated benchmark EffVLA matches the strongest published VLA; on the robustness benchmark it leads on most perturbation axes, and by the widest margins exactly where the language-initialized head is built to help. Standard LIBERO has compressed the top tier into a 9696–99%99\% band, and EffVLA sits inside it at 98.2%98.2\% (Table 4, baselines drawn from Yang et al. [37]), 0.40.4 points behind ABot-M0 and ahead of OpenVLA-OFT. LIBERO-Plus separates the same models: EffVLA (mean 79.8%79.8\%) leads on six of the seven perturbation axes, with its largest margins on the spatial and language axes that the language-initialized head was built to help, in particular camera viewpoint (+7.9+7.9 points over ABot-M0) and robot initial state (+37.9+37.9 over OpenVLA-OFT). It trails only on sensor noise, where the simpler MLP head was already strongest in our own ablation (Table 3). This external comparison is consistent with the within-study ablation.

Real-robot deployment on SO-ARM101.

The recipe transfers, unchanged, to a physical robot. We instantiate EffVLA on the low-cost SO-ARM101 open-source 6-DOF arm using the same single-pass L1 head copied from Qwen2.5-3B, with no axis of Section 3 retuned for the new embodiment; only the data pipeline changes, with Stage A run on the SO-ARM101 community corpus in place of DROID and Stage B on teleoperated demonstrations of the five tasks, merged and trained jointly so that one model serves all of them. Across five language-specified sorting tasks spanning one, two, and three objects handled in sequence, it succeeds on 4040 of 5050 trials, with success falling from 10/1010/10 on the single-object tasks to 5/105/10 on the three-object one. Figure 7 shows a representative rollout, and Appendix K gives the task suite and per-task results. We report this as a feasibility and transfer result rather than a comparative one: we do not run the alternative action heads on hardware, so these trials show that the LIBERO-selected recipe carries over to a new embodiment, not that it remains the preferred choice there.

Why we stop at ll, and what smaller variants cost.

The recipe does not have a larger version. Finding 3 already established that scaling any module past ll leaves success rate flat while latency keeps climbing, so a larger EffVLA provides no measurable benefit. If a deployment instead needs a smaller or simpler model, reducing action-head capacity offers the most favorable accuracy–latency trade-off: a smaller head walks the recipe down the accuracy and latency curve of Figure 6, and replacing the transformer stack with a single MLP regression layer (the OFT substrate) costs only about 11 point at the same latency. As a side benefit of the L1L_{1} family, EffVLA also tolerates skipping the DROID pretraining stage: at V=L=A=lV\!=\!L\!=\!A\!=\!l it loses only ∼2{\sim}2 points without it, against ∼22{\sim}22 for the flow-matching substrate (Appendix E), which is what makes the brief Stage B sufficient for the SO-ARM101 deployment above. The per-axis cost of any other single deviation from the recipe is in Appendix F.

7 Conclusion

We presented a controlled, latency-paired study of modular vision-language-action models. Across the tested configurations, action-head initialization is more influential than additional decoder complexity: VLM-initialized heads consistently outperform randomly initialized ones within the L1 comparisons, while flow matching and repeated inference provide little additional benefit once this initialization is used. Representation analyses further show that VLM-initialized heads remain more similar to the language backbone, suggesting that backbone compatibility helps explain these gains. Initialization also changes where scaling is most effective. After VLM initialization, the action head provides the largest measured accuracy gain per unit latency, with returns saturating near the scale used by EFFVLA. These results suggest that efficient VLA design should prioritize compatible initialization and allocate capacity according to measured module-level accuracy-latency returns.

8 Limitations

The four most consequential limitations of our study are the following. Benchmark and failure mode. LIBERO-Plus is short-horizon simulation, and we already observe a relevant failure within it: the plain MLP head beats EffVLA on sensor noise (Table 3). Finding 3’s saturation past ll may therefore not hold on harder, longer-horizon, or higher-precision tasks where larger backbones could repay (e.g. RoboCasa, real long-horizon mobile manipulation). Statistical resolution. The sweep trains one seed per cell; we re-train the l/l/ll/l/l anchor pair under five seeds (Appendix I), where run-to-run variation is 1.21.2–1.51.5 points. Sub-point gaps are therefore not significant, and the per-axis rankings on the harder perturbations should be read with that in mind; the initialization effect itself is the one result we can show is not configuration-specific, holding in all ten initialization-matched pairs (Appendix J). Real-robot evidence. The SO-ARM101 deployment is one task on one cheap 6-DOF arm and validates that the recipe transfers without modification, but does not establish generalisation to bimanual, mobile, or high-precision platforms. Alignment is an interpretation, not a demonstrated cause. We read the design space through the action head’s representation alignment with the VLM, and the attention and weight-space analyses of Appendix M support that reading, but our study manipulates alignment only through initialisation, so we cannot separate “alignment is the operative variable” from “these particular pretrained weights are”; a K-rank truncation probe was inconclusive under the LIBERO-Plus ceiling. The decisive control is a head initialised from the same backbone weights with the alignment destroyed (permuted layers, or a random orthogonal rotation), which should collapse both the CKA and the gain if alignment is what matters; we leave it to future work. Finally, the KV-share interface is held fixed across all transformer-block substrates, so the rules may not survive a different VLM–policy connector. Appendix N expands each point with concrete next steps.

Appendix A Implementation and Training Details

Substrate implementations.

The eight named substrates of Section 3 are built as follows.

  • •

    Fast (autoregressive trunk): decodes action chunks as language tokens through Qwen2.5 itself, using the FAST frequency-domain action tokenizer [26]. Inference is standard autoregressive decoding through the language backbone; the substrate has no separate stack and VLM-init therefore does not apply.

  • •

    OFT (MLP regression on VLM hidden states): reads VLM hidden states at the action positions through an MLP-ResNet head and predicts continuous action chunks with an L1L_{1} loss. The MLP has 1010M / 3030M / 8080M parameters at sizes ss / mm / ll. The architecture is not compatible with copying a transformer layer, so VLM-init does not apply.

  • •

    Transformer-block stack with KV-share. The four substrates OFT-TF, EffVLA, π0\pi_{0}, and π0\pi_{0}-vlminit all stack transformer blocks on top of the VLM and read the language backbone’s KV cache directly via a KV-share interface, so the action stack does not duplicate the VLM forward pass. The block hidden dimension is tied to the language-backbone hidden dimension; per-cell depths are tabulated in Table 8. Only π0\pi_{0} uses the DiT variant [25], whose block carries adaptive layer-norm conditioning on the denoising timestep; OFT-TF, EffVLA and π0\pi_{0}-vlminit all use the plain block. Within the L1L_{1} pair this means the random-initialization control and VLM-init share an identical architecture and only the weights differ.

  • •

    VLM-init. For EffVLA and π0\pi_{0}-vlminit we copy the parameter tensors of the last DD transformer layers of Qwen2.5-3B into the DD action-head layers. Architectural compatibility (matching hidden size, head count, and attention pattern) is enforced by construction.

  • •

    Flow matching (π0\pi_{0}, π0\pi_{0}-vlminit). The transformer stack is trained on a noisy action trajectory with the rectified-flow objective [19, 23] and integrated for four denoising passes at inference time, each applying a fixed-step update with the same parameters. Two caveats apply to the flow-matching contrasts. First, π0\pi_{0} uses the DiT block and π0\pi_{0}-vlminit the plain block, because the copied backbone layers have no adaptive layer-norm parameters to fill. The two therefore differ in block type as well as in initialization, so unlike the L1L_{1} pair this contrast is not initialization-only, and the mild −2.2-2.2-point effect of VLM-init under flow matching may reflect the change of block rather than a property of flow matching itself. Second, we hold the schedule fixed at four passes and do not sweep the number of denoising steps.

  • •

    Four-pass L1L_{1} (OFT-TF-r4, EffVLA-r4). The same transformer stack is invoked four times at inference, with the output of pass ii feeding the input of pass i+1i\!+\!1; training back-propagates through the four passes. No noise schedule is used; the repeat is purely a compute match to the four-pass flow-matching schedule, so the loss-versus-passes contrast in Section 3 is well-defined.

Two-stage training pipeline.

Every cell follows the same pipeline. Stage A (action-head pretraining) trains on DROID [10] with the public SigLIP2 and Qwen2.5 backbone checkpoints loaded but frozen, for the action-head architecture under study. Stage B (full-VLA fine-tuning) trains on LIBERO [20] for 100100k optimizer steps with every module unfrozen. Evaluation runs LIBERO-Plus [6]: four task suites ×\times seven perturbation axes, ∼1,000{\sim}1{,}000 rollouts per cell. Optimizer, learning rate, batch size, data augmentation, and chunk size (88) are held identical across cells.

EffVLA specifics.

EffVLA is the OFT-TF-vlminit substrate at V=L=A=lV\!=\!L\!=\!A\!=\!l: a 44-layer transformer-block stack initialized from the last 44 transformer layers of Qwen2.5-3B, on a SigLIP2-So400m vision encoder at 256256-pixel input. The head adds ∼0.35\sim\!0.35B parameters, for a full model of ∼3.75\sim\!3.75B. Training follows the same Stage A++B pipeline. For the SO-ARM101 real-robot deployment (Section 6) only the data pipeline changes: Stage A uses the SO-ARM101 open-source community corpus in place of DROID, and Stage B fine-tunes on teleoperated demonstrations of the five deployment tasks, merged into a single training set so that one model serves all five.

Appendix B Latency Measurement Protocol

Hardware and runtime.

All wall-clock latency measurements use an NVIDIA RTX 5090 in bf16 with batch size 11 and action chunk size 88. Each model is compiled with torch.compile before timing; no further kernel fusion, custom CUDA kernels, or quantization is applied. KV-share is implemented by reusing the language backbone’s KV cache via standard attention masking, so the transformer-block action stack adds neither a duplicate prefill nor a duplicate KV computation to the language forward pass.

Timing.

After compilation, each cell is timed over 100100 runs and we report the mean; the per-cell standard deviation is below 11 ms in every measured cell. Differences below 11 ms are treated as below the measurement-noise threshold throughout the paper.

What is and is not included.

The reported latency covers the full forward pass from a pre-tokenized image and instruction to the produced action chunk: vision encoding, language backbone forward, action-head forward (with the four-pass schedule integrated where applicable), and the FAST action de-tokenization in the autoregressive case. Image preprocessing, environment interaction, and tokenizer lookup are excluded because they are deployment-target-dependent rather than properties of the model.

Appendix D Module Scaling Analysis

This section breaks the aggregate Figure 5 sweep down two ways and characterises the architectural caveat that the ρ\rho values in Section 5 carry. In both breakdowns the three substrates and the colour scheme of Figure 5 are kept; reading off any panel reproduces the substrate ordering visible in the aggregate.

Per-task-suite breakdown.

Figure 8 marginalises the same module-scaling sweep over the four LIBERO-Plus task suites separately. The aggregate ordering of Figure 5 holds within every suite: the action head (AA) axis separates EffVLA from OFT and π0\pi_{0} on every suite, with the steepest substrate-specific rises sitting on the longer-horizon long-1010 suite where harder tasks leave the most room for the head to help. No suite reverses the qualitative picture: action-head scaling under VLM-init is the dominant per-suite trend, and the language and vision sweeps remain relatively flat once the head is fixed.

Per-perturbation-axis breakdown.

Figure 9 reorganises the same data along the seven LIBERO-Plus perturbation axes, and shows that the gains module scaling buys are concentrated rather than uniform. On the visually-saturated axes the pretrained backbones already handle (background textures, object layout, lighting), every module’s curve is flat to within a few points; almost all of the headroom sits on the harder axes (camera viewpoint, sensor noise, robot initial state). The distribution of gains across modules is itself informative: scaling LL helps camera viewpoint and language instructions most, scaling VV helps sensor noise most under the regression-head substrates, and scaling AA under EffVLA is the strongest single lever on robot initial state and camera viewpoint. A practitioner targeting a specific perturbation weakness can read off the relevant panel rather than treat module size as a uniform efficiency lever.

Depth–width coupling under KV-share.

On the four KV-share substrates the action stack’s hidden dimension is tied to the language backbone’s hidden dimension hLh_{L}, so hitting a comparable A=lA\!=\!l parameter target across LL scales forces the head depth to scale as D∝hL−2D\propto h_{L}^{-2}. Table 8 lists the configured depths and the resulting latencies and success rates for every LL scale at V=A=lV\!=\!A\!=\!l. EffVLA’s single-pass schedule keeps the LL–latency relationship monotone; π0\pi_{0}’s four-pass schedule multiplies the depth penalty 4×4\times and inverts it, so L=sL\!=\!s becomes slower than L=lL\!=\!l overall. The ρ\rho value for the LL axis under π0\pi_{0} that Section 5 would otherwise report therefore mixes the language-backbone effect with this architectural depth–width coupling, and we do not summarise it with a single slope.

Appendix E Effect of Pretraining

This is the only table in the appendix that reports cells trained without DROID action-head pretraining (Stage A); every other result in the paper uses the standard two-stage pipeline with Stage A. Table 9 reports the LIBERO-Plus 4-suite mean for every cell that we ran both with and without DROID action-head pretraining (Stage A). Two patterns hold. First, the L1L_{1} family (OFT) is largely robust to dropping Stage A: typical drops are 11 to 66 points, with the smallest scales showing the smallest gap (and one case of mild reversal). Second, the flow-matching substrate (π0\pi_{0}) consistently loses 1515 to 2222 points across scales when Stage A is removed. This contrast is the basis of the Section 6 statement that EffVLA inherits the L1L_{1} family’s pretraining robustness, which in turn is what makes the small Stage B sufficient when the recipe is retargeted to a new embodiment (Section 6, real-robot deployment on SO-ARM101).

Appendix F Cost of Deviating from the Recipe

Table 10 lists the cost of deviating from EffVLA along each single axis, measured against the recipe’s anchor (79.8%79.8\% on LIBERO-Plus, 39.239.2 ms on RTX 5090). Every entry is one cell of the Section 3 factorial, so no additional runs are required. The rows are grouped into two blocks. Substrate captures the head-design axes the main text Findings 1 and 2 are about: dropping VLM-init, replacing L1L_{1} by flow matching, replacing the transformer stack by an MLP, and running four passes instead of one. Module scale captures the per-axis cost of shrinking AA, LL, or VV from ll while leaving the other two at ll.

Appendix G VLM Backbone Capability

For context only: Table 11 reports general multimodal capability scores of the (SigLIP2, Qwen2.5) backbone pairs used in our sweep on six standard VLM benchmarks (MMBench-EN/CN, SEED, OCRBench, TextVQA, MMMU, AI2D, HallusionBench). Higher is better. These numbers are not used as a metric in any of the paper’s claims; they are included so a reader can map our {Vs,m,l,Ls,m,l}\{V_{s,m,l},L_{s,m,l}\} labels to their corresponding off-the-shelf VLM capability, and confirm that the larger backbones we sweep over are genuinely more capable on standard multimodal tasks.

Appendix H Cross-Benchmark Replication on SimplerEnv

We repeat the substrate comparison on a second benchmark and embodiment, SimplerEnv on a WidowX arm [17], with the action-head axes unchanged. Four substrates, 2424 trials per task over 44 tasks, 9696 trials per model.

The randomly initialized head here is architecture-matched: the same Qwen2.5 decoder layers are deep-copied and then re-drawn, so topology, parameter count and latency are identical to EffVLA and only the weight values differ. That contrast is 54.254.2 against 61.561.5, +7.3+7.3 points, next to +7.1+7.1 on LIBERO-Plus, which places the gain in the weights rather than in the head’s architecture or capacity. The three strongest substrates again fall within a few points of each other (61.561.5, 60.560.5, 59.459.4) and OFT and π0\pi_{0} swap order between benchmarks, so we read them as tied here as well. At 9696 trials per model the standard error on a difference is ≈7{\approx}7 points, so this is a replication of the effect size and the ordering, not an independent significance test.

Appendix I Repeated-Seed Check on the Anchor Pair

The sweep trains one seed per cell, so we re-trained the V=L=A=lV\!=\!L\!=\!A\!=\!l anchor pair from scratch under five seeds to measure run-to-run variation directly. Seed 1 is the run reported throughout the paper.

Two things follow, and they pull in opposite directions.

Run-to-run variation exceeds our one-point criterion.

The initialized head varies by 1.21.2 points (SD) across seeds and the MLP head by 1.51.5. The ∼1\sim\!1-point threshold we use elsewhere bounds evaluation noise only; training variation at a single cell is larger, so single-cell gaps of one or two points should be read as suggestive rather than decisive. This applies to the per-axis breakdowns and to the gg-scale comparisons in particular.

The EffVLA–OFT gap is small but consistent.

EffVLA leads in all five seeds, by +0.5+0.5 to +1.7+1.7 points (mean +1.1+1.1); under a null in which the two heads are equal, five same-signed differences in a pre-specified direction is a 1/321/32 outcome. We report this as a small and consistent advantage, not as a headline: the case for the transformer head rests on the initialization contrast and on its scaling headroom, both of which are several times larger than this gap.

Appendix J Single-Seed Training, and What Replaces a Seed Study

A multi-seed study of all 6363 cells was out of reach; Appendix I reports five seeds at the anchor pair instead. What we can report across the sweep is how often the initialization effect reappears when everything else changes. Table 14 lists every L1-regression pair of cells in the study that differ only in the action head’s initialization, holding the decoder, parameter count, latency, module scales and inference budget fixed.

All ten differences are positive, with a mean of +5.8+5.8 points. Under the null hypothesis that initialization has no effect, the sign of each difference is a fair coin, so ten same-signed differences give a two-sided sign test p=0.002p=0.002 (restricted to the nine LIBERO-Plus pairs, p=0.004p=0.004). The one near-zero case, +0.8+0.8 at A=sA\!=\!s, is the smallest action head in the sweep, which is what the account in Section 4 predicts: a head with few layers has little capacity to inherit into.

We state plainly what this does and does not bound. It shows that the effect is not an artifact of one configuration: it survives changing the vision encoder, the language backbone, the action-head size, the inference budget, the benchmark, and the embodiment. It does not bound the run-to-run variance of a single cell, which only repeated training seeds can measure and which we do not have. A reviewer asking for seeds is asking about the second quantity, and we do not claim to have answered it.

Appendix K Real-Robot Evaluation Protocol

Platform and data.

We instantiate EffVLA unchanged on the SO-ARM101 low-cost open-source 6-DOF arm: the same 44-layer transformer-block head copied from the last four layers of Qwen2.5-3B, single-pass L1, read through the same KV-share interface, with no axis of Section 3 re-tuned for the new embodiment. Only the data pipeline changes. Stage A action-head pretraining uses the SO-ARM101 community’s open-source teleoperation corpus in place of DROID, and Stage B fine-tunes on demonstrations we collected by teleoperating the arm on the five target tasks, merged into one training set: a single model is evaluated on all five, not one model per task.

Task suite.

The workspace holds three objects, a yellow cube, a blue marker, and a blackboard eraser, together with three compartments of increasing size. Each task is issued as a single natural-language instruction naming every object and the compartment it belongs in, so difficulty is set by how many objects must be handled in one instruction rather than by the difficulty of any individual grasp. Table 15 gives the five instructions verbatim.

The multi-object tasks are the informative ones. A single instruction names two or three object–compartment pairs, so the policy has to track which pairs it has already satisfied and re-ground the instruction on the remaining ones; an error early in the sequence is not recoverable and the episode is scored as a failure.

Success falls monotonically with the number of objects that must be handled in sequence, from 10/1010/10 and 9/109/10 on the single-object tasks to 5/105/10 on the three-object one. This is the expected shape for a policy executed open-loop over a long horizon: the per-object success rate stays high, but the episode requires every stage to succeed, so errors compound.

What this experiment does and does not establish.

We report the real-robot trials as a feasibility and transfer result, not a comparative one. We do not train and evaluate the alternative action heads (OFT, a randomly initialized transformer head, or a flow-matching head) on the same hardware, so these trials show that the recipe selected on LIBERO carries over to a different and much cheaper embodiment with the design axes unchanged; they do not establish that it remains the preferred configuration in the physical setting. A like-for-like on-hardware comparison is the natural next step and is the evidence a stronger deployment claim would need.

Appendix L Additional Attention Rollouts

This appendix supports the aggregate instruction-attention result of Section 4 (Figure 4) with the token-level detail and four further single rollouts.

Token-level detail.

We measure attention at the action head’s first layer (L0, the layer nearest the backbone) over 128128 rollouts, 6464 per condition, spanning the four LIBERO-Plus task suites at the V=L=A=lV\!=\!L\!=\!A\!=\!l cells. The word ranking in Figure 4b covers instruction words only: the chat-template role tokens that wrap the prompt are not part of the instruction and are excluded. They are not negligible: the assistant role token alone attracts the single largest share of the VLM-init head’s text attention (0.0960.096 mean per-token mass, against 0.0050.005 under random initialisation), more than twice the highest-ranked instruction word, so the aligned head attends both to where its answer begins and to the words that name the task. We report the template tokens here rather than plotting them, since including them in the ranking would conflate prompt structure with task grounding.

Per-rollout examples.

Figures 10 and 11 show four further single-rollout examples in the same format as Figure 3, one from each LIBERO-Plus task suite. In every case the VLM-init head places several times more mass on the instruction than the random-initialised head and concentrates it on the object and location nouns that name the task (bowl, ramekin, cream cheese, wine bottle, rack, mug, microwave), while the random head leaves the instruction almost unattended and spreads its vision attention diffusely across the scene.

Appendix M Weight-Space Alignment: Additional Detail

This appendix expands the CKA analysis of Figure 2 with the per-module breakdown. Because the L1L_{1} transformer-block head is architecturally identical to a backbone block, its projections share the backbone’s shape, so the CKA between each action-head projection and the corresponding backbone layer is well-defined. Read per module on the V=L=A=lV\!=\!L\!=\!A\!=\!l cells, the K++V “backbone-information” and output projections are preserved most (CKA 0.790.79 and 0.810.81) while the query path Q adapts most (CKA 0.540.54), consistent with the head keeping what the backbone reads while re-purposing how it attends, the weight-space counterpart of the instruction-attention behaviour in the main text (Figure 3).

We read this evidence as correlational. It accounts for the attention behaviour and the success-rate pattern, and it is what motivates reading the whole design space through alignment, but we manipulate alignment only through initialization, so it does not establish that alignment, rather than these particular pretrained weights, is the operative variable (a K-rank truncation probe was inconclusive under the LIBERO-Plus ceiling). The decisive control would initialize the head from the same backbone weights with the alignment destroyed, by permuting the layers or applying a random orthogonal rotation per matrix, holding the weight statistics fixed: if alignment is what matters, both the CKA and the +7.1+7.1 gain should collapse to the random-init level. It is consistent with the cross-module transfer results of Kumar et al. [13], Lee et al. [14].

Appendix N Limitations and Extended Discussion

This appendix expands the main-text Limitations section (Section 8) with the supporting evidence, the failure modes we observe, and concrete steps that would extend the claims.

Why action-head scaling depends on initialisation (Finding 2).

Section 5 shows that action-head scaling returns about 44 success points per ms only when the head inherits the language backbone’s weights, and roughly a third as much when it does not. The interpretation that fits the numbers is that the transformer blocks behave as an extension of the language backbone when they inherit its weights, and as an isolated decoder when they do not, so added capacity is converted into accuracy in the compatible case and largely into latency in the isolated one. This is consistent with the transfer-learning results of Kumar et al. [13], Lee et al. [14] discussed in Section 2, and Appendix M supplies direct weight-space evidence for it (the language-initialized head stays aligned with the backbone at CKA 0.760.76 against 0.240.24 for random init, and attends to the instruction where the random head does not); what remains open is the causal-intervention side, since the one truncation probe we ran was inconclusive under the LIBERO-Plus ceiling. Whether the same coupling extends to other modular pretrained systems (multimodal fusion stacks, tool-using agents, retrieval-augmented models) is also not something we test here.

Backbone-family specificity.

Every cell in our experiment uses SigLIP2 as the vision encoder and Qwen2.5 as the language backbone, so the +7.1+7.1-point initialisation gain rests on the assumption that Qwen2.5’s last transformer layers are useful when used as action-head initial conditions. Other VLM families differ in normalisation (RMS vs. LayerNorm), positional encoding (RoPE vs. ALiBi vs. sinusoidal), and attention pattern (GQA vs. MHA vs. MLA), and any of these could change the size or even the sign of the initialisation effect. The most direct way to test this is a replication on a Llama-3- or Gemma-2-based backbone using the same factorial; we treat the present experiment as the controlled measurement on one backbone family rather than a universal claim.

Benchmark scope and a measured failure mode.

LIBERO-Plus is simulated and emphasises short-horizon manipulation; the saturation past ll that we read off Figures 5–6 is therefore a saturation on this benchmark. Two concrete failure modes are visible already. First, on the Sensor Noise perturbation axis the plain MLP head (OFT) beats EffVLA by 1313 points (Table 3, 79.479.4 vs. 66.166.1). Second, the per-task-suite breakdown (Figure 8) shows that long-10 has the steepest substrate-specific rises and is the suite least saturated by ll. We expect harder, longer-horizon, or higher-precision benchmarks (e.g. RoboCasa, mobile manipulation, real long-horizon kitchen tasks) to re-open the case for larger models; a replication on at least one such benchmark is the natural next step.

Statistical resolution.

Each of the 6363 cells in the sweep uses a single random seed; the l/l/ll/l/l anchor pair is additionally re-trained under five seeds (Appendix I), where run-to-run variation is 1.21.2–1.51.5 points. We therefore treat sub-point success-rate gaps as not significant and do not claim ordinal rankings on the harder perturbation axes where multiple cells sit within 11–33 points of each other. A seed-variance budget on the eight V=L=A=lV\!=\!L\!=\!A\!=\!l ablation cells (Table 3) plus the three deployment-relevant module-sweep curves would tighten Findings 2 and 3 considerably; we did not run it under the present compute budget.

Architectural caveat: the KV-share interface.

All four transformer-block substrates share the same VLM–policy interface: the action stack reads the language backbone’s KV cache directly. This interface is what makes the L↔AL\!\leftrightarrow\!A depth–width coupling of Appendix D unavoidable and what makes VLM-init architecturally clean (since the head and the backbone have identical block shape). We did not ablate the interface itself. Whether the rules survive under a Q-former, cross-attention, or learned-query connector is an open question, and the most informative replacement experiment would compare KV-share against one alternative connector while holding everything else fixed.

Hardware specificity of the latency analysis.

All wall-clock latencies are measured on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090 in bf16 with batch size 11. On edge hardware (Jetson Orin, mobile NPUs) the per-module latency ratios shift because vision encoders and language backbones have different memory-bandwidth profiles, and the action-head dominance of Finding 2 may compress or invert. A multi-platform latency replication (a server GPU, an edge GPU, a mobile chip) would establish whether the recipe’s Pareto-optimality is platform-independent.

Real-robot evidence.

The SO-ARM101 deployment validates that the recipe transfers without architectural change to a real embodiment. But the evidence is one task on one inexpensive 6-DOF arm, with the brief teleop fine-tuning the Section 6 description allows. We do not claim generalisation to bimanual, mobile, or high-precision platforms (e.g. Franka, Aloha, mobile-manipulator stacks); a broader real-robot evaluation across embodiments and task families is the most consequential gap to close.

Fixed inputs.

We hold the input image resolution at 256256 px and the action chunk size at 88 throughout. Both affect the action-head’s task in non-trivial ways: a longer chunk lengthens the parallel decode the language-initialised head is performing, and a higher resolution changes the visual-token budget the vision encoder produces. A sweep over {4,8,16}\{4,8,16\} chunk sizes on EffVLA would be the cleanest stress test of Finding 2, since action-head scaling is what we predict should benefit most.
